articles.summary: On the recent EU Service Boundary Release webinar we explored how this new capability helps organizations operating in the European Union have more control over their data and who can access it. Financial service and insurance organizations that operate in the European Union face a range of cloud compliance obligations under DORA, EBA outsourcing guidelines, and NIS2 that go beyond “data residency.” Regulators, auditors, and internal risk and procurement teams now expect proof of who can access customer data, where those personnel are located, and how third-party ICT risk is documented and governed. The Pega EU Service Boundary (EUSB) addresses this by combining EU-resident operations, in-boundary data storage, and client-controlled encryption (BYOK) for financial service and insurance organizations. What's actually at stake For most industries, a cloud compliance gap is a procurement headache. For financial services and insurance, it's existential. Customer financial data, transaction histories, behavioral analytics used for personalization, underwriting data, claims records, and KYC and AML files are some of the most sensitive, most regulated data in the European economy. When this data is exposed, mishandled, or can't be accounted for during an audit, the consequences compound quickly: Regulatory penalties. DORA's incident reporting and ICT risk management obligations mean a poorly governed third-party relationship can create real exposure fast. Remediation and audit costs. A failed regulatory audit in financial services can run into the millions of euros once you factor in remediation, fines, and the disruption of corrective action plans. Stalled deals and renewals. Security and procurement reviews increasingly stall the moment a vendor can't clearly answer who has access to production data and from where. That's lost time and, in competitive RFPs, lost business. Customer and market trust. Policyholders and account holders are trusting you with their financial lives. A sovereignty or access-control gap that becomes public is a reputational event, not just a compliance one. The answer most vendors give today, “your data is stored in the EU,” doesn't close any of these risks anymore. Which EU regulations govern cloud data sovereignty for financial services and insurance? DORA (Digital Operational Resilience Act) is the one keeping most CISOs and compliance officers up at night right now. It requires financial entities to maintain a detailed register of information on every ICT third-party provider, manage concentration risk, test operational resilience, and report significant ICT-related incidents on tight timelines. Cloud and SaaS vendors supporting critical functions fall squarely inside its scope. EBA Guidelines on Outsourcing Arrangements require banks to assess, document, and continuously monitor outsourcing risk, including where data is processed and who can access it, with heightened scrutiny for “critical or important” functions. NIS2 extends cybersecurity and incident-reporting obligations across critical sectors, financial services included, raising the bar on how operational access and security controls must be governed and evidenced. Together, these frameworks ask financial services and insurance organizations to answer questions that go well beyond storage location. Who operates the systems? Can you demonstrate least-privilege access? Can you prove, with evidence, how exceptions are handled? Can you complete an outsourcing risk assessment without chasing five different teams for answers? How the EU Service Boundary addresses DORA and EBA requirements This is the gap the Pega EU Service Boundary was built to close. Customer financial data and behavioral analytics stay in-boundary. If you're using Pega Customer Decision Hub to personalize offers, or Pega Know Your Customer and Client Lifecycle Management to manage onboarding and due diligence, that data, along with Cloud Data Storage, Cloud File Storage, Decision Data Storage, and backups, is stored and processed within the AWS European Sovereign Cloud in Germany, operated exclusively by EU-resident personnel. Claims, disputes, and investigations stay accountable. For insurers running Pega Smart Dispute or Pega Smart Investigate, the EU Service Boundary gives you a documented, auditable record of who touched sensitive claims and investigation data, and from where, shortening the evidence-gathering your compliance and audit teams currently do by hand. Your DORA third-party register gets easier to complete. The EU Service Boundary clearly defines what data lives inside the boundary and what, like business contact data or support case data, is handled as a global resource outside it. That clarity helps your ICT risk and outsourcing teams document the relationship with the specificity DORA and EBA guidance expect. Your most sensitive data is protected even from privileged access. With Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) encryption, your organization, not Pega, holds the Key Encryption Key. Even privileged operations personnel can't access BYOK-protected fields without your authorization. Where to go from here Every financial service and insurance organization is navigating this from a different starting point: different regulators, different legacy infrastructure, different timelines for DORA compliance or your next outsourcing review. There isn't a generic answer to where your gaps are. That's a conversation worth having directly. Reach out to your Pega account team or contact us to talk through your specific use cases, your current regulatory pressure points, and whether the EU Service Boundary is the right fit for your organization. Want to go deeper on Pega's approach to security and compliance? Visit pega.com/trust. Join the Conversation If this session sparked ideas or questions for you, we'd love to continue the discussion. Join the Pega-as-a-Service Expert Circle — our community hub for monthly webinars, peer knowledge-sharing, and direct access to Pega's cloud and delivery experts: Pega-as-a-Service Expert Circle. The Q&A conversation from this session is also open — post your follow-up questions there, and our team will respond. Additional questions that weren't answered live will be picked up in upcoming Expert Circle webinars.

articles.summary: Pega as-a-Service Q3 2026: Release and Roadmap Highlights On October 15, 2026, the Pega as-a-Service Expert Circle hosted its quarterly Pega Cloud release and roadmap webinar. I moderated the session, and Satya Mishra, Head of Pega Cloud Infrastructure, Updates, Security and Monitoring, took us through what is new and what is coming next. The session was for clients, partners and consulting teams who want to understand where Pega Cloud is heading, and it ended with a panel discussion and live Q&A. If you missed it, you can watch the recording here. A faster, smarter Infinity '26 The session opened with the Infinity '26 release. Satya highlighted Infinity Studio, which brings developer agent choices such as Copilot or Claude together with Pega Blueprint best practices. He also covered governed orchestration of humans, bots and third-party AI agents, and Customer Engagement Studio in Customer Decision Hub for generating campaigns and real-time decisioning. On pricing, he explained that Pega charges a flat fee per case rather than per token, because of the token efficiency of its AI design. Updates made easier with My Pega Cloud The new Assess Update feature in My Pega Cloud scans the release notes against the product stack installed in your environment. It then summarizes the changes, rule impacts and upgrade considerations that matter to you. When you proceed, an updated clone environment is created. You can run your test suites there before you schedule the update of your other environments. Satya also presented the Innovation Sandbox Program, a dedicated Infinity '26.1 sandbox for up to 15 users for 90 days at no additional cost. You request it through msp.pega.com. Global footprint and the EU Service Boundary Pega Cloud now runs across 44 regions on AWS and GCP. Thailand, Indonesia and Paris/France were added recently, New Zealand (Auckland) is in progress, and Querétaro, Mexico is planned for next year. The EU Service Boundary is now live on the AWS European Sovereign Cloud in Brandenburg, Germany. Data storage, operations and resident personnel are all EU-based, and customers can bring their own keys. Pega CDH support is planned by the end of Q4. Enhanced Disaster Recovery, which gives full multi-region failover for mission-critical workloads, is now also available for CDH and on GCP. Security, storage and observability Satya covered inbound IP allow listing and studio lockdown. You can restrict Infinity Studio, Dev Studio, App Studio and Admin Studio to your developer IP ranges. A pilot of inbound mutual TLS starts in Q4. On storage, he stressed keeping case attachments in Cloud File Storage rather than in the database. A database downsizing capability is now available for migrated clients and for clients running large archival projects. Log streaming to Dynatrace is generally available on AWS and is expanding to GCP by the end of the year. Deployment Manager and PDC Deployment Manager as a Service now offers native test execution for Constellation applications, GenAI-assisted test generation and risk review, and a pilot for syncing masked production data to non-production environments. In Pega Diagnostic Center (PDC), the new Queue Processor monitoring, HTTP metrics and a redesigned CDH landing page give teams much better visibility. Four short demos you can watch on their own The webinar included four live demonstrations, and each is available as a separate video: Cloud Update demo Secure Inbound Access demo PDC demo Pega Labs demo What the audience asked The live Q&A covered granular role privileges in Deployment Manager as a Service, a view of all followed cases in PDC, and MCP support for Deployment Manager and PDC. Satya said MCP is not on this year's roadmap but he wants to evaluate it for next year. He also said Pega is open to adding roles and permissions once it knows what is missing. For PDC, he said a much richer version is planned, built around actionable insights. You can read the full discussion in the [Q&A conversation]([LINK: Q&A discussion post]). Join the conversation This session is part of an ongoing series, and there is more to come. Join the Pega as-a-Service Expert Circle to get access to additional webinars and related content, and to share your own cases with peers and Pega experts. Do you have a question the session did not answer, or a use case Pega should hear about? Add it to the Q&A conversation or start a new thread. Please also complete the post-webinar survey, because your answers shape the next agenda. Recommended resources Webinar replay: Pega as-a-Service Q3 2026 Release & Roadmap Q&A conversation Demo videos (Cloud Update, Secure Inbound Access, PDC, Pega Labs) Don't Forget JOIN THE CONVERSATION on Pega-as-a-Service Expert Circle

articles.summary: They Don't Get It: The One-Case-Type Anti-Pattern Is Succeeded by the One-Agent Anti-Pattern The Dynamic Work Design Approach from 2018 by Repenning and Kieffer from MIT is becoming even more important in the Age of Agentic AI. The Anti Pattern A long-standing anti-pattern in workflow design is the one-case-type solution: one component built to deal with every variant of a request, wrapping heterogeneous work into a single structure so that its differences never have to be separated. The case type holds routine approvals, exceptions, and edge cases side by side, with branches so deep that nobody can say which path is correct. In the age of agentic AI, the same error returns in a new form. The one-agent solution is one agent given every tool, a broad brief, and responsibility for the whole case. It looks efficient for the same reason the one-case-type design does: there is one thing to build and one thing to govern. In practice, it overloads a single agent with tasks that need to be handled separately, and it removes the accuracy that specialization would provide. The people who build either design don't get it. They optimize for the number of components, when the design question is how the work should be divided. The continuum between generalism and specialism Every component sits somewhere on a continuum between generalism and specialism. A generalist handles many kinds of work with one configuration. A specialist handles one kind of work with a configuration tuned to it. Neither end is wrong in itself. The error is choosing a position on the continuum by default, usually toward generalism, because a generalist is one thing to build. Poor design happens when the split is not made in either place. In work design, the variants of a request that need different handling are not separated into distinct paths. In solution design, the component that performs the work is not separated into distinct units, each suited to one kind of task. The result is a component that is too general to be accurate and too coupled to be changed. Judgment is not only agentic The continuum applies to judgment itself, and judgment does not have to be performed by a language model. A deterministic rule is judgment made explicit: a decision table that says what happens when a claim exceeds a threshold and the policy is in force. It is the most predictable form of judgment, because its logic can be read, tested exhaustively, and audited. A machine learning model is judgment learned from data: a score that estimates risk or classifies a pattern from many labeled examples. It is probabilistic, but its behavior can be measured against held-out data and monitored for drift. A language model agent is judgment over unstructured input: reading a free-text complaint, weighing evidence in a document, or drafting a response. It is the most flexible form, and the hardest to predict. Each form fits a different kind of judgment, and the right choice follows from the nature of the decision. Where the criteria are known and stable, a rule is the specialist. Where the criteria must be learned from patterns in historical data, a model is the specialist. Where the input is open-ended language and the output needs reasoning, an agent is the specialist. Using an agent for a decision a rule could make is the one-agent anti-pattern in its purest form: a generalist tool applied to work that has a more precise specialist. It adds cost and unpredictability to a decision that did not need either. There are places where you don't need AI. If you know your business rules, you should not have an agent derive them again. A rule costs no tokens and behaves the same way every time, which a language model cannot guarantee. AI belongs where rules run out: interpreting unstructured requests, extracting data from documents, summarizing a case, and researching similar cases. This changes the split. In a well-designed workflow, the judgment units are not only agent steps. Some are decision tables, some are model scores consulted by a rule, and only some are agents. The Pega architecture supports this mix: the same case can call a deterministic decision, a scored prediction, and an agent step, each in the stage where its judgment is needed. The design question is therefore not whether to use an agent, but which kind of judgment each unit requires, and whether the rule, the model, or the agent is the most specialized tool for it. Why the one-agent design fails An agent's accuracy depends on several things that can be tuned: the instructions it follows, the model it uses, the context data it receives, and the tools it can call. A generalist agent must compromise on all four. Its instructions must cover every task, so none is precise. Its model must serve every task, so none is optimal. Its context must hold data for every task, so none is focused. Its tools must cover every task, so each invites the wrong use. A specialist agent can be tuned on each of the four. Its instructions name one judgment. Its model is chosen for that judgment. Its context carries only the data that judgment needs, and its tools are only the ones it uses. Its behavior can then be tested against a golden reference set for that specific outcome. A generalist agent offers no such outcome to test against, and its failures are hard to attribute, because a fix to its prompt affects every path at once. Agents cannot repair a design that was never split. Placing an agent into a mixed workflow asks it to handle both predictable and unpredictable work, and no improvement in the model changes that. The split has to come first. Why splitting is the design The Repenning argument supplies the principle. In an MIT Sloan Management Review article, Nelson Repenning, Don Kieffer, and James Repenning argue that work should be designed so that its well-defined and ambiguous parts are separated and handled in the way each requires. Stable work suits a serial, factory-style design, and ambiguous work suits a collaborative, studio-style design. Forcing both into one process means it must be efficient and adaptive at once, and it ends up being neither. Their practical advice maps directly onto component design. Separate well-defined work from ambiguous work. Keep units small enough to check often. Know who helps when something fails. Build explicit triggers and checks between the modes. Each is an argument for splitting rather than merging, in the workflow and in the agent that serves it. Splitting also makes change cheaper and failure visible. A new exception can be added to one unit without retesting the rest. A failure in a specialist belongs to a named unit with its own owner and escalation path, instead of appearing as a vague problem in the whole process. How this looks in Pega Pega's case management model supports the split at the castype level. A parent case owns the outcome and coordinates. Child cases each cover one unit of work with their own stages and rules, and the parent can close only when they are resolved. Exceptions are handled by alternate stages, reached through a defined condition or user action rather than by additions to the normal path. The parent-to-child handoff uses the Create Case shape, which can create one child, or one child per entry in a page list. The parent can then hold with a Wait shape until the child resolves, using the case dependency option. A child counts as resolved when its status starts with "Resolved." Data passing deserves care: the Create Case shape supports a data transform for initial values, but community reports suggest the source page parameter field may not appear in every release, so pass only what the child needs and confirm the mechanism for your version. Agents attach to these units at specific steps. Pega's Agent Step runs inside a case type and performs one defined action asynchronously, so the case keeps moving. A GenAI Connect rule suits a single fixed action, while an Agent Step suits a judgment task. Either way, the agent is a specialist inside a workflow that already has a trigger in front of it and a check after it. What to avoid Three patterns recur. The first is one case type that holds every variant of a request. The second is one generalist agent given all the tools and a broad brief. The third is an exception handled by a workaround in the normal path, which hides it from both the design and the people who must review it. Each has a split as its remedy: a separate case type or child for each distinct kind of work, a specialist agent for each distinct judgment, and an alternate stage for each distinct exception. Where to start Take one existing case type and list its variants. Separate the variants that rules can decide from those that need judgment. Give each group its own case type or child case. For each judgment group, define the one task the agent performs, the data it may see, the tools it may call, and the field where its output lands. Then define the exception routes as alternate stages with named triggers. Only after that split should you ask whether an agent is needed, and where. In most workflows, the answer is yes for a smaller share of the work than the original design implied, and the parts that remain are easier to build, test, and govern. The people who don't get it treat the workflow, and the agent that serves it, as one thing to build. Both are several things with different properties, and the architecture should reflect that. References Nelson P. Repenning, Don Kieffer, and James Repenning, "A New Approach to Designing Work," MIT Sloan Management Review, sloanreview.mit.edu/article/a-new-approach-to-designing-work/. 2018 A New Approach to Designing Work AI Use / Disclosure: This work represents my own ideas, objectives, expertise, and professional judgment. articles.summary: Agentic AI Architecture for Enterprise Scale: Design Before You Build Most organizations building agentic systems treat architecture as an afterthought. They focus on prompt engineering, model selection, and capability. They build the agent, test it, and only then ask: "Now how do we integrate and align this into our enterprise architecture?" This is backwards. Enterprise-grade agentic systems require architectural decisions made upfront, not retrofitted later. The difference between a working pilot agent and a production-grade autonomous system running across your enterprise is architecture. Research on enterprise AI adoption shows that this matters. Gartner's analysis of enterprise AI implementations finds that approximately 80% of AI pilots fail to scale—typically not due to technology limitations, but due to operationalization and governance gaps. McKinsey's research on enterprise AI governance demonstrates that organizations with explicit governance frameworks built into system design show 40% higher implementation success rates. This is architecture working as intended. This article walks you through what enterprise agentic architecture actually means and how to design systems that scale reliably, stay governed, and deliver measurable business outcomes. The Gap: Pilot Agent vs. Enterprise Agent Let me illustrate with something I see across every customer engagement. A pilot agent works like this: Team builds an agent to solve one problem Agent calls a service, gets a response, returns an answer Works great in a sandbox environment with test data Team declares victory An enterprise agent must work like this: Agent receives ambiguous input from multiple channels Agent must interpret intent, handle missing information, route appropriately Agent executes with governance controls and audit trails Agent escalates to humans when confidence is low or risk is high Agent is monitored for drift and quality degradation Agent's decisions are measurable and traceable Agent integrates with existing processes and case management Agent scales to thousands of instances across business units Agent remains predictable and controlled as scale increases The difference isn't the technology. It's the architecture. Most organizations move from scenario 1 to scenario 2 by adding requirements one at a time. Each requirement is bolted on: "Oh, we need to add a harness." "Oh, we need to add more human oversight." "Oh, we need to address some of the points from Enterprise Architecture and the AI Governance Board." This creates fragile, complex systems that break under scale. Enterprise organizations need to start with scenario 2. They design for governance, oversight, measurement, and scale from day one. Everything else flows from that foundation. What Enterprise Agentic Architecture Means Enterprise agentic architecture is the structure that enables predictable autonomous decision-making at scale. It answers: Strategic Questions: Which business processes are candidates for agentic automation? What level of autonomy is appropriate for each decision? How do governance and oversight integrate with agent execution? Structural Questions: How should agents be orchestrated (single agent vs. multi-agent)? How do agents interact with existing systems and processes? Where do humans intervene in the agent's decision flow? How is data (context, decisions, outcomes) managed and traced? Governance Questions: How do compliance requirements shape agent behavior? How are decisions audited and explained? How does the system detect and respond to drift or failure? Measurement Questions: How do you measure agent reliability before production? How do you measure business impact after deployment? How do you ensure agents improve processes, not just automate them? Architecture is what connects all these questions into a coherent system. Five Architectural Principles for Enterprise Agentic Systems Based on what I've observed across various customer engagements, discussions with practitioners, industry peers, and in articles, publications and research, here are the principles that separate enterprise-grade systems from pilots that fail to scale. 1. Governance-First Design Don't build agents first, then add governance. Design governance into the architecture from day one. The EU AI Act (2024) requires high-risk autonomous systems to maintain human oversight and audit trails. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework emphasizes that governance must map directly to engineering controls. This isn't regulation-as-burden, it's a description of what enterprise systems must look like. Architecture is how you make it operational. This means: Decision authority is architecturally clear: What can the agent decide autonomously? What requires escalation? Control points are built in: Where can the organization override or pause agent decisions? Audit trails are structural: Not added as an afterthought, but baked into every decision path. Explainability is designed in: Agents don't just decide—they prepare explanations and evidence. In practice: The agent architecture includes a declarative rules layer that governs what the agent can decide. The agent proposes structured decisions. The rules deterministically approve or escalate the proposals. This is architecture. It's not bolted on; it's foundational. 2. Process-Aware Design Don't architect agents in isolation. Design them to fit into and improve existing business processes. Process mining research (van der Aalst, 2020) demonstrates that understanding current workflows - not just automating tasks - is foundational for intelligent automation success. Enterprise systems that ignore process intelligence and context (including the traces, it's distributions, related objects aso) inevitably fail because they optimize for agent capability rather than measurable business outcome. This means: Understand the process first: What are the current pain points in a process? Design agent responsibilities clearly: What part of the process should the agent own? What stays with humans? Integrate with case management: Don't create separate agent workflows. Integrate with existing case/workflow management systems. Measure process impact: Success isn't "agent works." It's "process measurably improves." In practice: We often see teams automating individual steps without understanding the broader process and it's challenges holistically. They automate a small part (e.g. intake classification) brilliantly, but downstream routing is manual or the biggest effort or cost driver isn't addressed. Process-aware architecture means designing the agent's work as part of an end-to-end process flow. 3. Human-Centered Escalation Don't design humans out. Design humans in strategically. Research on human-AI collaboration (Amershi et al., 2019) demonstrates that human oversight is most effective when AI systems provide clear reasoning, confidence scores, and supporting evidence. This isn't a feature, it's an architectural requirement and a usability and experience topic. When you design escalation strategically, humans become more effective, not less. This means: Escalation is architectural: When humans should intervene is a design decision, not an afterthought. Context is prepared: When you escalate to humans, you prepare context, evidence, and recommendations. Authority is clear: Who decides what at each escalation level? Feedback loops exist: How do human decisions teach the agent? In practice: The best multi-agent systems don't maximize agent autonomy. They optimize for "appropriate autonomy", autonomy matched to risk, confidence, and reversibility. If a decision is reversible and low-risk, the agent decides. If it's irreversible or high-stakes, humans decide with agent recommendations. 4. Observable Design Design systems you can see into. Observability is architectural. This means: Every decision is traceable: What did the agent do? Why? With what confidence? Behavior is monitorable: What patterns are emerging? Is the agent drifting? Quality is measurable: Before production (golden dataset testing), during production (silent testing), and ongoing (runtime monitoring). Failures are visible: Not hidden in logs, but surfaced systematically. In practice: When confidence drops below a threshold or patterns shift, teams should be alerted. That's not a feature bolted on to the agent. That's architectural from day one. 5. Multi-Agent Coordination Design for complexity. A single agent is rarely the answer. This means: Agent responsibilities are scoped: Each agent has a clear job. Not a monolithic "do everything" agent. Orchestration is explicit: How do agents hand off to each other? How do they share context? Conflict resolution is designed in: When agents have competing goals, how is conflict resolved? Learning is systemic: How do insights from one agent improve others? In practice: At Pega, the MCP (Multi-Channel Orchestration) framework enables this kind of architecture. You have specialized agents for intake, classification, routing, execution. They coordinate through explicit interfaces, not implicit dependencies. Two Reference Architecture Patterns Let me ground this in specific patterns that work at enterprise scale. Pattern 1: The Gated Agent (High-Oversight) When to use: High-risk decisions, regulated industries, mission-critical processes. Architecture: Input → Agent (Proposes) → Rules (Approve/Escalate) → Case (If escalation) → Human (If needed) → Execution → Monitoring (Outcomes & Drift) How it works: Agent proposes a decision with reasoning and confidence Declarative rules evaluate the proposal (does it pass governance checks?) If approved by rules, agent executes If not approved, escalates to case management for human review All decisions logged and monitored Why it works: Governance is structural. Humans never lose visibility. Decisions are auditable. Pattern 2: The Cooperative Agent (Moderate-Oversight) When to use: Moderate-risk decisions, operational efficiency, customer experience. Architecture: Input → Agent A (Intake) → Agent B (Classify) → Agent C (Route) → Case (Execution) → Monitoring How it works: Multiple specialized agents handle different parts of the process Agents coordinate through explicit handoffs Humans monitor the workflow and intervene when needed System learns from human interventions (e.g. annotations and silent evaluation) Why it works: Specialization reduces complexity. Handoffs are explicit. Humans are positioned at key decision points. How Architecture Enables Governance This is the critical point: Architecture is how governance becomes operational. Too many enterprises separate these concerns. They build agents over here. They build governance structures over there. Then they try to bolt them together. Enterprise architecture makes governance a structural property of the agent system, not a layer on top of it. Here's what that means in practice: Decision Authority (Architectural) Agent can decide if: • Confidence > 90% AND • Decision is reversible AND • Customer risk score < threshold Otherwise: • Escalate to human This isn't a policy. It's architecture. It's built into the agent's execution flow. Audit Trail (Architectural) Every decision captures: • What the agent decided • Why (reasoning) • Confidence level • Supporting evidence • Who approved (if escalated) • Outcome (what happened next) This isn't added later. It's structural from day one. Measurement (Architectural) System continuously measures: • Agent reliability (accuracy on golden dataset) • Process impact (cycle time, cost, quality improvements) • Business outcomes (revenue, satisfaction, risk) • Drift (does agent behavior change over time?) This isn't reporting. It's built into how the system operates. When governance is architectural, it's efficient, auditable, and effective. When it's bolted on, it's friction, complex, and fragile. The Measurement Question: How Do You Know It Works? Enterprise architecture must support measurement at three levels: Level 1: Agent Reliability (Does the agent work?) Golden reference testing (pre-deployment) Silent testing (early production) Runtime monitoring (ongoing) Level 2: Process Impact (Does the process improve?) Cycle time (faster?) Cost (cheaper?) Quality (better?) Customer experience (more satisfied?) Level 3: Business Outcomes (Does the enterprise win?) Revenue impact Risk reduction Compliance improvement Competitive advantage Most organizations obsess over Level 1 and ignore Levels 2 and 3. Enterprise architecture must support all three. Practical Steps: Design Your Agentic Architecture If you're building agentic systems in your enterprise, here's how to approach it: 1. Start with Process Intelligence Before you design the agent, understand your current process. Where are the inefficiencies? Where do decisions happen? Where do humans add value vs. friction? Process and Task Mining and Analytics are very helpful here to build a data backed view! 2. Define Decision Authority What decisions can be autonomous? What requires human judgment? What's the criteria for each? 3. Design for Governance First What governance structures must exist? Build them into the architecture, not on top of it. 4. Choose Your Reference Pattern Gated (high-oversight) or Cooperative (moderate)? Most enterprises start with one of these two patterns. 5. Build for Observability Design systems you can see into. Every decision should be traceable and measurable. 6. Plan for Multi-Agent Coordination Most enterprises need multiple agents. Design the orchestration and handoff patterns upfront. 7. Define Measurement (All Three Levels) How will you measure agent reliability, process impact, and business outcomes? The Enterprise Reality Building agentic systems is not primarily a technology problem. Your models work. Your frameworks work. Your infrastructure works. The problem is architecture. Most organizations are trying to retrofit enterprise requirements onto systems designed for pilots. The organizations that will scale agentic AI predictably are those that design for enterprise from day one. They start with governance. They design for oversight. They architect for measurement. They plan for scale. Architecture is how you make that happen. RESEARCH FOUNDATION This article is grounded in regulatory requirements, academic research, and industry practice. Here's the research backing enterprise agentic architecture: Regulatory Frameworks The EU AI Act (2024) requires high-risk autonomous systems to maintain human oversight and audit trails. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework explicitly calls for governance to map to engineering controls. ISO/IEC 42001 requires organizations to establish AI governance systems. These aren't optional guidelines—they're regulatory requirements that enterprise agentic architecture must satisfy. Academic Research Research on human-AI collaboration (Amershi et al., "Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction," Microsoft Research, 2019) demonstrates that oversight is most effective when systems provide clear reasoning and confidence. Process mining research (van der Aalst, "Process Mining: Data Science in Action," 2020) establishes that understanding workflows is foundational for intelligent automation. Multi-agent systems research (Weiss, "Multiagent Systems," 2013) confirms that agent coordination requires explicit architectural design. Industry Research Gartner's analysis shows that approximately 80% of AI pilots fail to scale—typically due to operationalization gaps, not technology limitations. McKinsey research on enterprise AI governance demonstrates that organizations with explicit governance frameworks built into system design show 40% higher implementation success rates. This validates that architecture, not post-deployment governance, drives success. Standards & Frameworks IEEE standards for autonomous systems governance (IEEE 7000-7004) align with these principles. Enterprise architecture frameworks like TOGAF establish that architecture must drive governance and operational effectiveness. BPMN process modeling standards inform how we design agents within business processes. Key Takeaways Architecture comes first—before building agents, design the system that governs, oversees, and measures them. Governance is structural—not a policy layer on top, but part of how the agent system works. Humans stay in control—through architectural escalation, not bolted-on oversight. Process context matters—design agents into existing processes, not in isolation. Measurement is multi-level—agent reliability, process impact, and business outcomes. Multi-agent systems are normal—design orchestration patterns upfront. Observability is non-negotiable—build systems you can see into and trace through. The difference between a working agent and a working agentic enterprise is architecture. Design it right from the start. articles.summary: From AI Governance to AI Value Assurance: Why Enterprises Need to Govern Value, Not Just Risk A governance framework answers one question perfectly (Can we trust it?) but leaves another equally important one unanswered (Is it creating measurable value?). Governance without value assurance is expensive risk management. The Governance Trap An organization builds an AI governance framework. It includes: ✅ AI policies and principles ✅ Risk classification matrix ✅ Approval workflows ✅ Human oversight requirements ✅ Audit and monitoring controls ✅ EU AI Act compliance procedures But here's what nobody's measuring: ❓Did the process actually improve? ❓Is cycle time faster? ❓Is cost lower? ❓Is customer satisfaction higher? ❓Did we actually create the value we said we would? The governance framework answers "Is this system trustworthy?" perfectly. It doesn't answer "Is this investment paying off?" These are different questions. And they require different controls. The Board's Two Questions when approving AI When your board evaluates an AI investment, they're actually asking two questions: Question 1: Can we trust it? Will it fail safely? Is it under control? Can we explain its decisions? Are we compliant? Do we understand the risks? Question 2: Is it creating value? Is the business outcome materializing? Can we measure it? Is the ROI positive? Are we competitive? Should we scale this? Your governance framework answers Question 1 brilliantly. Most organizations don't have a coherent answer to Question 2. Why This Matters Now Three things have converged: First: Governance is maturing. Organizations are building AI governance frameworks. Policies are in place. Compliance is being met. The "Can we trust it?" question is increasingly well-answered. Second: Scale is accelerating. Organizations are moving from "we have a few AI systems" to "we're building 50+ AI systems." At that scale, you can't measure value one system at a time. You need a portfolio approach. Third: The market is shifting. Enterprises that can prove AI value will get investment. Enterprises that can't won't. This is especially true as CFOs become more skeptical and boards demand ROI. The competitive advantage goes to organizations that can credibly answer "Yes, it's creating measurable value—and here's the proof." Enter: AI Value Assurance. What Is AI Value Assurance? AI Value Assurance is the discipline of proving business value while managing risk, at scale, across an enterprise AI portfolio. It's different from governance. Governance manages risk and control. Value assurance proves value and measures impact. Together, they answer both board questions. Here's what Value Assurance requires: Clear intent about what value you're trying to create Evidence that the system can create that value before you make it autonomous Operational controls that keep it reliable at scale Measurement that proves the value is real This isn't bolt-on. It's structural. It changes how you design, deploy, and govern AI systems. The Four-Level AI Value Assurance Model I propose organizing AI Value Assurance into four levels. Each level answers a specific question and requires specific evidence. Level 1: Value Intent The question: What business outcome are we actually trying to achieve? What's the baseline? This is where most organizations fail. They start with "Let's automate this process" without asking "Will automating this actually create the value we think?" Value Intent requires: Clear definition of the business outcome (cycle time reduction? Cost savings? Risk reduction?) Baseline measurement of the current state Target definition of the desired future state Success criteria for the AI system In practice: A financial services organization wanted to automate loan approval. The real business outcome wasn't "faster approval"—it was "higher approval rate without higher loss ratio." That's a different optimization target. Value Intent made that explicit from day one. Governance connection: Your policies should require explicit Value Intent before approval. If you can't articulate what business outcome you're optimizing for, the system shouldn't be approved. Level 2: Evidence Before Autonomy The question: Can we trust this system to deliver that value? This is where evaluation happens. You gather evidence that the system can actually do what you're asking it to do—before you give it autonomy. Evidence Before Autonomy requires: Golden reference testing on representative data Silent testing in parallel with human decisions Business outcome testing (not just accuracy—does it improve the business process?) Human review before autonomous decisions In practice: Before a healthcare organization let an agent triage patients autonomously, they ran silent testing for two weeks. The agent made triage recommendations while humans made the actual decisions. That evidence proved the agent was reliable enough for autonomy. Governance connection: This is where your human oversight, escalation, and quality controls live. You're building evidence, not just managing risk. Level 3: Operational Assurance The question: Can we keep it working at scale? This is where predictability comes in. Once the system is live and autonomous, you need controls that ensure it stays reliable, predictable, and under control. Operational Assurance requires: Governance structures that define decision authority Escalation procedures for edge cases and low-confidence decisions Monitoring for drift, degradation, and anomalies Controls that can pause or redirect the system if needed In practice: A manufacturing organization deployed an agent for preventive maintenance scheduling. Operational Assurance meant: The agent could schedule routine maintenance autonomously Edge cases (equipment failures, schedule conflicts) escalated to humans Daily monitoring tracked decision patterns and cost impact If costs spiked, the system could be paused while engineers investigated Governance connection: This is where your control tower lives—the centralized dashboard that lets you govern multiple AI systems simultaneously. Level 4: Value Realization The question: Is it actually creating the value we defined in Level 1? This is the critical question that most organizations leave unanswered. You measure accuracy, precision, recall—all technical metrics. But did the business outcome improve? Value Realization requires: Measurement of the business outcome (cycle time, cost, quality, revenue, customer satisfaction) Comparison to baseline (did it improve relative to Level 1 baseline?) Attribution (did this AI system cause the improvement, or was it other factors?) ROI calculation (is the value greater than the cost?) In practice: A customer service organization deployed an agent to handle routine inquiries. They measured: Technical metrics: Accuracy 92%, confidence calibration good Process metrics: Cycle time reduced 30%, escalation rate 8% Business metrics: Customer satisfaction increased 12%, cost per interaction down 40% ROI: System cost $200K/year, value delivered $1.2M/year The technical metrics looked good. The business metrics proved it was worth the investment. Governance connection: This is where your board gets their answer. Not "Is it working?" but "Is it creating value?" How the Four Levels Connect Here's the critical insight: you need all four levels, and they must be connected. Skip any level, and the model breaks: Skip Level 1 → You don't know what success looks like Skip Level 2 → You deploy untested systems Skip Level 3 → Systems degrade silently Skip Level 4 → You never know if it actually worked Most organizations do Levels 1-3 reasonably well (because of governance frameworks). They skip Level 4 or treat it as optional. That's the gap. Why This Matters for Chief Data Officers or Chief AI Officers If you're a Chief Data Officer or Chief AI Officer, you manage multiple AI systems. You need to answer two questions for each system: Is it under control? (governance) Is it creating value? (value assurance) At scale—50, 100, 500 systems—you can't answer these one by one. You need a framework. AI Value Assurance gives you that framework. It lets you govern for risk AND value simultaneously. It lets you explain to the board: "These systems are under control, delivering measurable value, and here's the evidence." How This Changes Governance Design If you adopt AI Value Assurance, your governance processes change: Current approach: Proposal → Risk assessment → Approval → Implementation → Monitoring → Deployed Value Assurance approach: Proposal with Value Intent → Risk + Value assessment → Approval → Evidence building (silent testing) → Implementation with Operational Controls → Measurement → Continuous improvement The difference: Value Intent and Value Realization become structural parts of governance, not afterthoughts. The Strategic Implication Here's what matters for your organization: Enterprises that can prove AI value at scale will: Get more investment for AI Scale faster Attract talent Compete more effectively Have strategic leverage with customers Enterprises that can't prove value will: Get scrutinized by CFOs Scale slower Struggle with ROI conversations Lose competitive ground The difference between these two futures is AI Value Assurance. Key Takeaways Governance isn't enough — It answers "Can we trust it?" but not "Is it creating value?" Value Intent is foundational — If you can't articulate the business outcome, the system shouldn't be approved. Evidence Before Autonomy is non-negotiable — Testing and silent mode prove the system can deliver before it's autonomous. Operational Assurance keeps it working — Controls and monitoring ensure predictability at scale. Value Realization proves the investment — Measurement shows whether the board's question gets answered: "Yes, it's creating value." These four levels must be connected — They're not sequential steps. They're an integrated system. At scale, you need a control framework — Managing 100 AI systems requires portfolio governance. Value Assurance provides it. The next phase of enterprise AI governance isn't more risk management. It's proving value while managing risk. That's AI Value Assurance. Research Foundation Governance Maturity & Value Measurement Organizations have spent 2+ years building AI governance frameworks aligned with EU AI Act, NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and ISO/IEC 42001. This focus on risk governance is necessary but incomplete. Research on AI value realization (McKinsey, "The state of AI adoption," 2023) shows that 60% of organizations deploying AI struggle to measure ROI—not because the technology doesn't work, but because they haven't established value measurement frameworks. Portfolio Governance at Scale Enterprise architecture research and control frameworks (TOGAF, enterprise risk management standards) establish that managing multiple systems at scale requires integrated governance models, not system-by-system approaches. AI governance is beginning to adopt this principle, but most enterprises haven't operationalized portfolio-level value measurement. Value Realization in Enterprise Transformations Research on business value from enterprise transformations (ERP, cloud migration, etc.) demonstrates that value capture requires: Clear baseline and target definition Evidence before full deployment Operational controls maintaining performance Continuous measurement and adjustment AI Value Assurance applies this proven pattern to AI systems. Further Reading Governance & Risk: EU AI Act (2024) NIST AI Risk Management Framework (2023) ISO/IEC 42001: AI Management Systems Value Measurement: McKinsey: "The state of AI in 2023" and "Measuring AI's Impact" reports Gartner: AI Value Realization reports Harvard Business Review: "The Business Value of AI" Enterprise Transformation & Scale: TOGAF 9 (Enterprise Architecture Framework) Enterprise Risk Management (COSO Framework) Business Value from IT Transformation studies AI Use / Disclosure: This work represents my own ideas, objectives, expertise, and professional judgment. articles.summary: For 2 years, I have created Blueprints using a screen reader. Like many blind users, I have become highly skilled at navigating complex applications, moving through pages, locating controls, and finding the information I need. It is simply part of how I work. When I first heard about creating a Blueprint through AI chat, I was skeptical. My initial reaction was that there was no way this approach would be easier. I assumed I would spend more time trying to understand what the AI was doing than actually building the Blueprint. I expected frustration. I expected confusion. Honestly, I assumed I would prefer the traditional approach. After building an entire Blueprint with AI, I changed my mind. More Than Just a Faster Way to Build One of the biggest differences between the traditional Blueprint experience and the AI-assisted experience was that the conversation became part of my learning process. In the traditional interface, I can complete tasks because I know where things are and how they work. However, the interface does not always explain why something should be configured a certain way. With AI, I could ask questions as I worked. If I was adding a step to a stage, I could ask why that step might be useful. If I was unsure about a particular configuration choice, I could ask for an explanation. The assistant didn't just perform actions. It helped me understand the reasoning behind them. I found myself wishing I had access to this type of guidance when I first started at Pega. I believe I would have learned the Blueprint process much faster because I would have understood the purpose behind the configuration decisions rather than simply following steps. The Learning Curve Was Real My experience was not immediately positive, initially, I was actually less efficient using AI. I had to learn how to interact with it. I needed to understand the pace of the conversation, how to ask questions effectively, and what kind of information the assistant needed from me. There were moments early on when I wanted to stop using AI and go back to creating the Blueprint manually because it felt faster. But something interesting happened as I gained experience. The more I used the assistant, the more natural the interaction became. I learned how to shape my requests, and the assistant became easier to predict. By the end of the testing, I felt that I was working more efficiently than I would have been manually. More importantly, I wasn't just completing tasks. I learned throughout the process. Why AI Was Different for Me as a Screen Reader User The greatest benefit was not speed. It was navigation. Traditional applications often require screen reader users to spend significant time moving around an interface, locating controls, finding the correct section, and keeping track of where they are on the page. Over years of using assistive technology, this becomes second nature, but it still requires effort. With AI, much of that effort disappeared. Instead of spending time searching for controls, I could remain focused on the conversation and ask the assistant to perform actions on my behalf. This fundamentally changed how I interacted with Blueprint. Rather than navigating to accomplish work, I could simply describe my intent. That may seem like a small difference, but for a screen reader user it can significantly reduce the cognitive effort involved in navigating a complex application. Another unexpected advantage was spelling. I have never been a particularly strong speller. When creating case types or entering names, the assistant frequently understood what I intended and corrected minor mistakes automatically. It may sound like a small feature, but it removed another source of friction from the process. Where the AI Assistant Fell Short The experience was not perfect. One of my biggest frustrations was the inability to duplicate workflows through AI. Since workflow duplication can already be performed manually within Blueprint, I expected the assistant to support the same capability. Instead, I found myself repeatedly trying to convince the AI to perform an action it could not do. I also encountered challenges when working with uploaded files. In one case, the only file available for testing was related to cars. When I attempted to add it to an existing case type, the AI refused because the file content did not match the case type. To complete my testing, I ultimately had to create a car-related case type simply so the assistant would accept the file. There were also times when the AI needed information that I did not realize was required. For example, when working in Workflow Details, I eventually learned that I needed to specify which case type I wanted to modify before asking certain questions. However, if I was new user, rather than waiting for me to discover what information was missing, the assistant should have proactively asked: "Which case type would you like to work with?" Small prompts like that could make the experience much more approachable for someone learning Blueprint for the first time. A Different Way of Thinking About Accessibility I have used JAWS for a long time, and historically I have preferred direct navigation. It is what I know. It is what I trust. What surprised me during this evaluation was realizing how quickly that preference is changing. The more I work with AI, the more comfortable I become relying on conversational interactions. That does not mean traditional accessibility is no longer important. Users still need access to the interface and the ability to navigate independently. But AI introduces a new interaction model that complements traditional accessibility rather than replacing it. For me, it often feels less like driving through the interface and more like collaborating with a knowledgeable assistant. Looking Ahead The experience also made me think about what AI could do next. I would love to be able to say "undo the last change" and have the system automatically reverse the most recent action. I would like AI to duplicate workflows, modify release planning information, and describe reports and charts in a meaningful text format. As a blind user, one of the most exciting ideas is having AI help navigate the application itself. Imagine being able to say, "Take me to Release Planning" or "Take me to the next step," and being moved directly to the area where work needs to happen. That would allow AI not only to perform tasks, but also to act as an intelligent guide through the Blueprint creation process. Final Thoughts When I started this evaluation, I expected to prefer the traditional Blueprint experience. By the time I finished, I would have chosen the AI-assisted approach. The reason is not simply efficiency. It is that the experience changed how I interacted with the application. The AI reduced navigation overhead, helped me learn as I worked, corrected small mistakes, and made the Blueprint process feel more conversational and approachable. For a blind user who has spent years navigating software through a screen reader, that is a significant shift. What began as an experiment in AI-assisted Blueprint creation ended up feeling like a glimpse into a different future for accessibility, one where understanding, navigation, and productivity can all happen through conversation.

articles.summary: At an ACAMS event in Frankfurt jointly sponsored by Pega and Moody's last week, attendees were asked a deceptively simple question: How many of the 22 predicate offence categories have a dedicated detection scenario in your organisation? The results were striking. Fewer than eight: 11%. Between eight and fourteen: 16%. Between fifteen and twenty-one: 11%. All twenty-two: around 5%. And by far the largest group, 58%, answered "don't know." At one level, that's understandable. Financial crime controls have become increasingly specialised. Transaction monitoring, sanctions screening, fraud detection, cyber monitoring, and customer due diligence often operate in separate systems, managed by different teams, using different methodologies. But the poll raises a more important question: How confidently can a financial institution trace a recognised financial crime risk from detection, through investigation, to an appropriate decision about the customer? That question matters because regulators increasingly expect firms not only to operate controls, but to demonstrate that those controls align with their financial crime risk assessment. The expectation is risk-based rather than checklist-driven. Institutions should be able to explain why certain risks are relevant to their customers, products, geographies, and channels, and show how those risks are reflected in monitoring, investigation, and due diligence processes. The challenge is no longer proving that controls exist. It's proving that they are appropriate, proportionate, and effective. The 22 categories, for those who need a refresher The 22 categories mentioned in the question are the ones identified in Directive (EU) 2018/1673, commonly known as the EU's Sixth Anti-Money Laundering Directive (6AMLD), which harmonised the criminal activities considered predicate offences for money laundering across EU member states. The list broadly aligns with the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) designated categories of offences and includes familiar risks such as fraud, corruption, tax crime, drug trafficking, and terrorism financing, alongside categories such as cybercrime and environmental crime that have taken on greater prominence in recent years. The regulatory logic is straightforward: money laundering is ultimately defined by its predicate. If monitoring programmes are heavily focused on a small number of typologies, institutions may be highly effective at detecting some forms of criminal proceeds while having little visibility into others. Many organisations monitor behaviour effectively. Far fewer can confidently explain how that monitoring maps to the financial crime risks they have identified. Why coverage is patchy, and why nobody knows how patchy Three factors make this question difficult to answer. First, most monitoring scenarios were never designed around predicate offences. They were designed around behaviours: structuring, rapid movement of funds, dormant account activation, unusual cash intensity, mule activity, or anomalous transaction patterns. A single scenario may support the detection of several different predicate offences simultaneously, making direct mapping difficult. Second, detection is fragmented across systems. Transaction monitoring sits in one platform, sanctions screening in another, fraud detection somewhere else, and cyber risk signals in another tool entirely. Each capability has its own ownership, coverage assumptions, and optimisation cycle. Third, and perhaps most importantly, the predicate offence is often identified, if at all, at the end of the investigative process. An alert is generated because of a behaviour. An investigator assesses the activity. A conclusion may eventually be reflected in a case outcome or SAR narrative. But that conclusion rarely feeds back into a structured process capable of showing where controls are working well, where coverage overlaps, and where gaps may exist. The result is that many institutions can describe their individual controls but struggle to explain how those controls collectively support their financial crime risk assessment. Closing the loop: where investigation management comes in This is where the discussion becomes less about detection and more about what sits above it. No financial institution will ever achieve perfect scenario coverage. Criminal methodologies evolve. New threats emerge. Detection technologies are specialised by design. The practical challenge is not achieving complete coverage. It's understanding what is being detected, learning from investigative outcomes, and using those insights to improve future controls. That requires an investigation capability capable of bringing signals together. Investigators need visibility of sanctions hits, fraud alerts, cyber indicators, transaction monitoring events, and customer information in the context of a single customer story rather than a collection of disconnected cases. They also need a consistent way of recording investigative outcomes so those outcomes can be analysed over time. This is where Pega Alert and Investigation Management (AIM) becomes relevant. AIM is designed to orchestrate investigations across multiple alert sources, business lines, and jurisdictions through a unified investigation framework, helping financial institutions consolidate customer risk information and manage investigations consistently across financial crime domains. When investigation outcomes are captured consistently, organisations are far better positioned to understand which risks are generating cases, which controls appear effective, and where optimisation efforts should be focused. The answer to the ACAMS question starts to become evidence-based rather than anecdotal. Knowing your client means knowing their predicate exposure There is a second dimension to this challenge, and it begins long before the first alert is generated. Not every customer carries the same predicate offence exposure. A timber importer carries environmental crime risk in a way a domestic payroll bureau does not. A crypto exchange sits closer to cybercrime and fraud proceeds than many traditional businesses. Clients operating in extractive industries in certain jurisdictions may present elevated corruption and tax crime exposure. Cash-intensive businesses can create exposure across several categories simultaneously. A genuinely risk-based approach means customer risk profiles should influence which risks institutions pay closest attention to and, ultimately, which controls are applied. That depends on KYC data that is rich enough to capture industry, geography, ownership structures, products, and behavioural indicators in a structured and usable way. The same principle applies before an alert is ever generated. Effective financial crime controls depend on understanding which risks are relevant to a customer in the first place. Pega Client Lifecycle Management and KYC (CLM-KYC) provides a framework for orchestrating onboarding, due diligence, and ongoing KYC processes across lines of business and jurisdictions, helping institutions maintain a more consistent and actionable view of customer risk throughout the client lifecycle. When customer risk profiles, monitoring controls, and investigation outcomes contribute to a shared view of risk, predicate offence coverage stops being an abstract compliance question. It becomes a practical one: For this customer, given what we know about them, which financial crime risks are we exposed to, and what are we doing to detect them? A question worth asking internally If your honest answer to the ACAMS question is "don't know," you're clearly not alone. The path to an answer is unlikely to involve building twenty-two new monitoring scenarios. Instead, it starts with connecting customer risk assessments, detection controls, investigative outcomes, and continuous improvement into a single risk-management feedback loop. Once that loop exists, coverage becomes visible. And once coverage becomes visible, the 58% becomes a number organisations can do something about.
